item.title: Before You Paste: Student Privacy and Choosing the Right AI Tool
item.description:
Part 2 of 9 in the series AI at a Small College.

It is 11 p.m., you have 30 essays left, and a free chatbot is one tab away. Pasting in a student’s essay to “get started on feedback” feels harmless. It may not be. Before any of the later posts in this series, it is worth spending ten minutes on what you may put into which tool.

This post is general guidance, not legal advice. Your college’s policies and counsel have the final word.

FERPA in plain words

FERPA, the federal student-privacy law, covers education records: grades, submitted work, advising notes, accommodation information and emails about a student, among others. You can see your own students’ records because you have a legitimate educational interest in them. Sharing those records with an outside company is different.

An outside service may receive education records without each student’s consent only if the college treats it as a “school official”. That means it performs a service the college would otherwise do itself, is under the college’s direct control over how the records are used and kept, and may not pass them on. In practice, that takes a contract.

Two misunderstandings are common:

  • “The company promises not to train on my data." A no-training promise is helpful, but on its own it is not the same as the college’s control over use, retention and deletion. Free personal accounts do not give the college that control.
  • “I removed the student’s name, so it’s anonymous." At a small college, often not. A course list, a project topic or a detail like “the only veteran in the class” can identify a student. Removing names is good practice. Do it, but don’t treat the result as anonymous.

The traffic-light rule

Most colleges already classify their data. Map those classes to AI tools like this, and post the table where you will see it.

Kind of information Examples Personal AI accounts College-licensed AI (under contract) College-hosted private AI
Green: public Catalog, published syllabi, public web pages, published papers Yes Yes Yes
Yellow: internal Draft committee reports, internal procedures No Yes Yes
Orange: confidential or student records Grades, student work, advising notes, personnel files, search materials No Only if your college approves that tool for this kind of data Only if your college approves it for this kind of data
Red: highly restricted Social Security numbers, financial-aid tax data, health and disability records, passwords No No No

Two rules sit on top of the table:

  • Never record tenure, promotion, grievance or conduct deliberations, whatever tool you use.
  • Don’t ask an unapproved tool to “remove the names” from identifiable text. By the time it removes them, it has already received them.

Which tools you probably already have

Most colleges already pay for at least one education-tier AI tool, often without announcing it:

  • Google campuses: the Gemini app and NotebookLM are “core services” in Google Workspace for Education, turned on by default for higher education since 2025. Google states that this data is not reviewed by humans or used to train its models.
  • Microsoft campuses: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat with enterprise data protection comes with the standard education licenses. The full Microsoft 365 Copilot is a paid add-on.
  • Contracted tools: ChatGPT Edu and Claude for Education are sold to institutions under contract. Whether student records may go into them depends on that contract.
  • College-hosted: some colleges run their own AI on campus servers. My college’s EMTutor pilot is one example. Data stays on campus, but the college is responsible for securing it.

Universities read the same product differently. One major university allows student records in ChatGPT Edu under its contract, while another advises against uploading academic records even with a license. Another found a data-sharing setting turned on by default in its workspace. So the only list that matters is your own college’s.

Try it this week

  1. Find your college’s approved-tools list. Search your IT or teaching-center website for “AI tools” or “approved software”. If there is no list, email IT one question: “Which AI tools are approved for FERPA-protected student information, and which only for public or internal information?" Until you hear back, treat everything except green as not allowed in AI tools.
  2. Sign in the protected way. Use the AI tool through your college account, not a personal one. In Copilot, look for the indicator that enterprise data protection is on. In Gemini or NotebookLM, check that the account in the corner is your college account.
  3. Fix your personal account settings. If you also use a personal ChatGPT account for public material, open Settings → Data controls and turn off “Improve the model for everyone”.
  4. Clean up. Look through your past chats in any personal AI account. Delete any that contain student work, grades or names.
  5. Practice de-identifying. Before pasting anything about students into an approved tool:
    • Remove names, ID numbers and email addresses.
    • Remove details that identify someone by context.
    • Summarize groups instead of individuals.
    • Don’t report on groups of fewer than five students.

For chairs and directors: a one-page policy

If your department or office has no AI policy yet, one page is enough to cover:

  • Approved tools. Which tools may be used with which kind of data (link the table above).
  • Responsibility. Whoever uses AI is responsible for the accuracy of what they submit.
  • Decisions. AI makes no final decisions on grades, admissions, hiring, discipline or financial aid.
  • Disclosure. AI use is disclosed where an outside body requires it.
  • Recording. Meetings are recorded only with consent, and sensitive deliberations never.
  • Incidents. Problems are reported to IT promptly.
  • Review. The policy is reviewed once a year.

Next time, with the rules settled, we start on the fun part: planning a course with AI, from learning goals to a first-draft syllabus.

Questions about your own situation? Write to me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

Sources

  • FERPA regulations, 34 CFR 99.31 (the “school official” and de-identification provisions)
  • US Department of Education Privacy Technical Assistance Center, Protecting student privacy while using online educational services
  • Future of Privacy Forum and Center for Democracy & Technology guidance on vendor contracts (FPF, CDT)
  • Google, Gemini and NotebookLM as core services for education and data protection
  • Microsoft, Copilot in education
  • Examples of differing university guidance: Carnegie Mellon, BYU, University of Illinois
  • Virginia Tech, Responsible use of AI in advising

item.title: Let AI Draft, You Decide: Where AI Actually Saves Faculty and Staff Time
item.description:
Part 1 of 9 in the series AI at a Small College.

Ask colleagues whether AI saves them time, and the answers split. Some say it has given them back an evening a week. Others say it has added work: checking what it wrote, rewriting what it got wrong, and worrying about students who use it. Both groups are right, and the research explains why.

This series is for faculty and staff in every discipline, not just computer science. Over the next three weeks, I will cover one area per post: protecting student data, planning courses, making materials, giving feedback, tutoring, advising, scheduling and committee work. Every post ends with steps you can try that week with tools your college probably already has.

AI use is now normal, but time savings are not

AI use among faculty grew quickly. In Tyton Partners’ national surveys, the share of instructors using generative AI at least weekly rose from 30% in 2025 to 52% in 2026. In the California State University system’s fall 2025 survey of more than 6,000 faculty, 55% said they use AI to develop course materials.

Time savings are a different story. Among instructors who use AI every day, 36% report a lighter workload, 39% report no change and 26% report a heavier one. Much of the extra work comes from dealing with students’ AI use. So far, no controlled study has measured how many hours faculty save on syllabi, slides or quizzes compared with doing the work by hand.

The studies that do measure time point to a pattern:

  • Repeatable tasks with a clear structure get faster. In one study, instructors took about 27 minutes to analyze their own course-evaluation comments. ChatGPT runs took 10 to 15 minutes.
  • Open-ended “help me with this” use can be slower. In a randomized study at a 2025 computing-education conference, teaching assistants who started from AI-drafted feedback took longer than those who wrote their own, and some let the AI’s mistakes through.

Gains go to people who build a repeatable routine, not to people who simply have access.

The rule: let AI draft, you decide

Across all the research I reviewed, one rule kept appearing. AI is good at producing first drafts: rewording, summarizing, organizing, generating options and explaining. It is unreliable at anything with a right answer that it cannot check:

  • Facts and requirements it was not given, such as a course prerequisite or a college policy
  • Dates, such as which weekday a holiday falls on
  • Citations: in one 2025 study, GPT-4o made up almost 1 in 5 of the references it produced
  • Judgments about people, such as grades, advising decisions and hiring

So divide the work. Let AI draft. Then let something you trust decide: the official catalog, your calendar, your rubric, a test, a colleague, your own expertise.

Three habits that make AI worth the time

1. Give it your material, not its memory. Upload your syllabus, the catalog or the reading, and tell it to work only from that. Then ask it to quote the sentence that supports each claim. That one instruction turns hidden guesses into things you can check in seconds.

2. One task per request. Ask for one learning goal, one quiz question or one paragraph at a time. In a 2025 study of AI-generated programming exercises, tasks covered every requested concept 94% of the time when they targeted one concept, but only 40% of the time when they targeted three. Small requests are easier to get right and easier to check.

3. Check it like a reviewer, and time yourself. Read every draft the way you would read a new colleague’s work: assume it is mostly right and look for the specific error. Write down how many minutes the task took. If AI makes a task slower or less accurate, stop using it for that task. That is a good result, not a failure.

Why this matters more at a small college

Small colleges use AI about as much as large universities, but have far fewer people to support it. Nationally, only about 1 in 10 chief academic officers report a central AI strategy at their institution, and only 6% of faculty fully agree that their institution gives them enough training. At a small college, a few people’s time is the scarce resource. A short, shared playbook is worth more than another tool license.

The series

Part Date Topic
1 Nov 23 Let AI draft, you decide (this post)
2 Nov 25 Before you paste: student privacy and choosing the right AI tool
3 Nov 27 Planning a course with AI: from learning goals to a draft syllabus
4 Nov 29 Course materials you can trust: quizzes, handouts, slides and accessibility
5 Dec 1 Feedback and grading: where AI helps and where it slows you down
6 Dec 3 A tutor for every student, without giving away answers or privacy
7 Dec 5 AI for faculty advisors: meeting prep without risking student records
8 Dec 7 For chairs: course offerings, teaching loads and schedules
9 Dec 9 Committee work, accreditation, and measuring the time you save

Try it this week

  1. Pick one task you do every week, such as writing a course announcement, summarizing a reading for discussion or drafting review questions. Choose something that uses no student information.
  2. Time yourself doing it the usual way once, and write down the minutes.
  3. Do it again with AI, using your college’s licensed tool (Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, ChatGPT Edu or Claude, signed in with your college account) and this prompt:
I will paste [my lecture notes / the reading / last week's announcement].
Using ONLY this material, draft [a 150-word announcement / five discussion questions / a one-paragraph summary].
After the draft, list each factual claim you made and quote the sentence from my material that supports it.
If a claim is not supported by my material, mark it [CHECK].
  1. Check the [CHECK] items, edit the draft and time the whole process, including your checking.
  2. Compare the two times. Keep the routine only if it was faster and at least as good.

Next time: what you may and may not paste into an AI tool, and how to find out which tools your college has approved.

Questions or examples from your own discipline? Write to me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

Sources

  • Tyton Partners, Time for Class 2025 and the 2026 report release
  • Inside Higher Ed, California State University faculty AI survey (fall 2025)
  • eCampus News, Faculty workload can drop with daily AI use (2025)
  • BMC Medical Education, AI analysis of course-evaluation comments (2024)
  • Ahmed et al., Augmenting teaching assistants with AI for programming feedback, SIGCSE 2025
  • Jacobs et al., Generating programming tasks with multiple concepts (2025)
  • JMIR, Citation fabrication by GPT-4o (2025)
